question: What is the mechanism of action by which the parasympathomimetic agents reduce intraocular pressure (IOP)?

options.A: circular ciliary muscle ﬁber relaxation with increased outﬂow through the trabecular meshwork
options.B: circular ciliary muscle ﬁber contraction with increased outﬂow through the trabecular meshwork
options.C: longitudinal ciliary muscle ﬁber contraction with increased outﬂow through the trabecular meshwork
options.D: longitudinal ciliary muscle ﬁber relaxation with increased outﬂow through the trabecular meshwork

explanation: Parasympathomimetic agents, or miotics, reduce the IOP by causing contraction of the longitudinal ciliary muscle ﬁbers where they insert into the scleral spur and trabecular meshwork. This contraction in turn improves outﬂow. There are 2 types of parasympathomimetic agents: direct-acting and indirect-acting agents. Direct-acting agents mimic acetylcholine at postganglionic parasympathetic junctions and other autonomic, somatic, and central synapses. Indirect-acting agents BCSC Excerpt References Notes.

question: What ocular condition are curvilinear tears in Descemet membrane most often seen in?
explanation: Tears in Descemet membrane (Haab striae) are seen because of a rapid stretching of the cornea in primary congenital glaucoma. They are not seen in congenital hereditary endothelial dystrophy (CHED) or Peters anomaly. Trauma from amniocentesis can result in a penetrating injury of the cornea. Tears in Descemet membrane can also be seen in a forceps injury sustained during delivery, but these are usually linear, not curvilinear.

question: In what type of glaucoma is a post- laser trabeculoplasty intraocular pressure (IOP) spike most common?
explanation: Patients with heavily pigmented trabecular meshworks are more prone to post-argon laser trabeculoplasty/selective laser trabeculoplasty (post-ALT/SLT) IOP spikes, due to greater absorption of the laser energy. One should use lower power and/or consider treating a smaller area when performing laser trabeculoplasty in pigmentary glaucoma patients. This phenomenon may also occur to a lesser degree with pseudoexfoliation (PXE) patients.

question: What is the most speciﬁc ophthalmoscopic sign of glaucomatous optic nerve damage?

options.B: asymmetric cupping of the optic nerves

explanation: The hallmark of glaucomatous optic neuropathy is progressive cupping of the disc. Cup-to-disc (C/D) asymmetry, focal rim loss, disc hemorrhages, and beta zone peripapillary atrophy may also represent early glaucoma. The term glaucoma refers to a group of optic neuropathies characterized by optic disc excavation, or cupping, and corresponding patterns of vision loss. The cup–disc ratio alone is not an adequate assessment of the optic nerve head (ONH) for possible glaucomatous damage. For example, a 0.7 cup–disc ratio in a large ONH may be normal, whereas a 0.3 cup– disc ratio in a very small disc is likely pathologic. Thus, assessment of the disc size is important; in healthy subjects, a small disc (vertical disc diameter < 1.5 mm) will have a small cup, whereas a large disc (vertical disc diameter > 2.2 mm) will have a large cup. Individuals of African ancestry, on average, have larger disc areas and larger cup–disc ratios than do white individuals, although substantial overlap exists.

question: How is uveoscleral outﬂow aﬀected by age, pressure, and cycloplegia?

options.A: pressure-insensitive, increases with age, increased by cycloplegic agents
options.B: pressure-sensitive, increases with age, decreased by cycloplegic agents
options.C: pressure-sensitive, decreases with age, decreased by cycloplegic agents
options.D: pressure-insensitive, decreases with age, increased by cycloplegic agents

explanation: Uveoscleral outﬂow is the nontrabecular outﬂow of the eye. It is pressure-insensitive and the predominant mechanism is one of aqueous passage from the anterior chamber into the ciliary muscle and then to the supraciliary and suprachoroidal spaces, exiting the eye through an intact sclera or along the nerves and the vessels that penetrate it. It can account for up to 45% of the total aqueous outﬂow. Uveoscleral outﬂow decreases with age and in patients with glaucoma. It is increased by prostaglandin analogues, and cycloplegic and BCSC Excerpt References Notes.

question: What commercially available topical beta-blocker is a selective ß-1 antagonist?
explanation: Of the 6 topical ß-adrenergic antagonists approved for use in the United States for the treatment of glaucoma (betaxolol, carteolol, levobunolol, metipranolol, timolol maleate, and timolol hemihydrate), only betaxolol is ß-1 selective. This medication may have fewer systemic side eﬀects in patients with pulmonary, central nervous system, or other systemic conditions, since it blocks largely cardiac (ß-1) activity and less pulmonary (ß-2) activity.

question: In what ethnic group is acute angle- closure glaucoma most prevalent?
explanation: Alaskan Inuits have the highest known prevalence of primary angle- closure glaucoma. East Asians also have a high prevalence of this disease and make up the majority of cases worldwide.

question: What adverse eﬀect of alpha agonists limits their utility in infants and young children?
explanation: Follicular conjunctivitis is the most common side eﬀect of ocular dosing of alpha agonists, and often precipitates cessation of the therapy. Granulomatous uveitis is a very rare side eﬀect. Xerostomia and lethargy are sometimes reported in adults, especially in the elderly. Central nervous system (CNS) depression including apnea, bradycardia, and systemic hypotension are life-threatening side eﬀects that can be seen in infants and young children using topical alpha agonists.

question: What corneal abnormality is commonly seen in Axenfeld-Rieger syndrome?
explanation: Posterior embryotoxon (visible in an anterior segment examination) is a prominent and anteriorly displaced Schwalbe line that is characteristic for Axenfeld-Rieger syndrome. Adhesions from the cornea to Schwalbe line can vary from threadlike and thin to broad bands of iris tissue. The remainder of the cornea in patients with this condition is otherwise normal. ﬁxation losses.

question: Automated static perimetry has several indices to gauge the reliability of a visual ﬁeld test. What reliability index measures how often the patient identiﬁes the stimulus in the previously placed physiologic blind spot?
explanation: The reliability of perimetry results is assessed by identifying the following patient response characteristics: Fixation losses: how often the patient identiﬁes the stimulus in the previously plotted physiologic blind spot location (ie, a response not expected), indicating that the eye is not aligned with the ﬁxation target. False-positive response rate: how frequently the patient signals when no target is displayed. False-negative response rate: how often the patient fails to signal when a target brighter than the previously determined threshold for that spot is displayed. Gaze tracker: tracks the pupil and checks for eye movements, which are signaled as upward deﬂections, and blinks, which are signaled as downward deﬂections.

question: In Ocular Hypertension Treatment Study (OHTS), what was identiﬁed as an important risk factor for the development of glaucoma in patients with ocular hypertension?
explanation: The Ocular Hypertension Treatment Study was the ﬁrst trial to prospectively document that thinner central corneal thickness was a risk factor for the development of glaucoma. In multivariate analysis, thinner central corneal thickness (CCT) emerged as a risk factor regardless of age, baseline IOP, or cup-disc ratio. This study underscored the importance of assessing CCT in all patients with ocular hypertension. Myopia, diabetes, hypertension, and heart disease were not associated with conversion to glaucoma.

question: Why is a gonioscopic lens required to visualize angle structures?

options.A: total internal reﬂection at the lens- aqueous interface
options.B: total internal reﬂection at the cornea- tear interface
options.C: total internal reﬂection at the cornea- aqueous interface
options.D: total internal reﬂection at the tear- air interface

explanation: Gonioscopy is required to view the angle structures because, at the tear-air interface, the critical angle (approximately 46 degrees) is reached in which light is totally reﬂected back into the corneal stroma. Use of a gonioscopic lens eliminates the tear-air interface, thus allowing for visualization of the angle structures.

question: A 67-year-old man presents with acute, painless vision loss in the left eye upon awakening. Visual acuity is 20/20 in the right eye and hand motions in the left eye. Intraocular pressure (IOP) is 28 mm Hg OD and 29 mm Hg OS without evidence of neovascularization of the iris or angle. The right eye fundus is normal; fundus ﬁndings in the left eye are seen in the ﬁgure. What ocular treatment could be considered to lower the risk of vision loss in the right eye?
explanation: Glaucoma and ocular hypertension are risk factors for the development of central retinal vein occlusion (CRVO). Consideration may be given to treating elevated IOP in a patient with a history of hemicentral retinal vein occlusion (HRVO) or CRVO in order to reduce the risk of a vein occlusion in the fellow eye. Panretinal photocoagulation would be an appropriate treatment for neovascularization secondary to a retinal vein occlusion. Anti–VEGF injections could also be used to treat neovascularization secondary to a retinal vein occlusion or macular edema from a vein occlusion. In this patient without evidence of neovascular glaucoma, anti–VEGF injections would not be eﬀective in treating the ocular hypertension in either eye. Topical steroids have no role in the treatment or prevention of retinal vein occlusion and could potentially increase intraocular pressure.

question: During the creation of a peripheral iridotomy, the 10 o'clock and 2 o'clock locations are avoided to decrease the risk of what complication?
explanation: Complications from iridotomy include bleeding, persistent postoperative inﬂammation, accelerated cataract formation, and lens damage. Retinal tear, postoperative IOP spike, and corneal endothelial damage can also occur. Visual dysphotopsias (glare, streaks, lines, halos) may be present and are thought to result from proximity of the iridotomy to the tear meniscus, which acts as a strong prism. Thus, some clinicians advocate temporal placement of the iridotomy, taking precautions to perform the iridotomy at a distance from the tear meniscus. However, it is unclear whether the location of the iridotomy aﬀects the likelihood of dysphotopsias, and a large prospective study suggests that it does not.

question: What region, as indicated by the arrows, consists of fenestrated connective tissue providing structural support for the optic nerve?
explanation: The lamina cribrosa lies in the laminar region of the anterior optic nerve. It consists of fenestrated connective tissue lamellae and provides the main structural support for the optic nerve as it exits the eye. It is made primarily of collagen; other extracellular matrix components include elastin, laminin and ﬁbronectin. Capillary beams nourish this critical region as the neural components of the optic nerve pass through the connective tissue beams. Two central fenestrations allow transit of the central retinal artery and vein. The connective tissue density within the lamina has been described histologically as lesser superiorly and inferiorly, as compared with the temporal and nasal aspects of the optic nerve. It has been suggested that these diﬀerences play a role in the development of glaucomatous optic neuropathy. The pores of the lamina cribrosa can be seen on ophthalmoscopy at the base of the optic nerve head cup. The nerve ﬁber layer of the retina is the most superﬁcial and anterior zone of the anterior optic nerve, composed of the axons of the retinal ganglion cells, visible with a red-free (green) ﬁlter. The next posterior layer is the prelaminar region, which lies adjacent to the peripapillary choroid. The laminar region is then continuous with the sclera and composed of the lamina cribrosa. The retrolaminar region is the most posterior segment of the anterior optic nerve and found immediately posterior to the lamina cribrosa. It is marked by the beginning of axonal myelination and is surrounded by leptomeninges of the central nervous system.

question: What is the mechanism of action of the Trabectome?

options.B: use an implant to create a low- resistance pathway between the anterior chamber and Schlemm canal
options.C: ablate the trabecular meshwork (TM) and inner wall of Schlemm canal
options.D: remove a strip of tissue from the trabecular meshwork (TM)

explanation: The Trabectome is used to ablate the TM and inner wall of Schlemm canal. The Kahook Dual Blade is used to perform an excisional goniotomy by removing a strip of tissue from the TM. Ab interno canaloplasty viscodilates the Schlemm canal. Trabecular bypass devices create a low-resistance pathway between the anterior chamber and Schlemm canal.

question: For a patient who develops aqueous misdirection (ie, malignant glaucoma) after cataract surgery, initial management would include what therapy?

options.D: laser disruption of the anterior hyaloid face

explanation: Initial medical therapy typically includes aqueous suppressants and cycloplegia, which may break or moderate an episode of malignant glaucoma or aqueous misdirection. If this therapy fails to elicit acceptable control of the intraocular pressure (IOP), then yttrium- aluminum-garnet (YAG) iridotomy may be performed, along with disruption of the anterior vitreous face in aphakic or pseudophakic patients. While medical management and laser iridotomy control malignant glaucoma in approximately half of patients, the rest will require surgical treatment. In these patients, pars plana vitrectomy with anterior hyaloido-zonulo-iridectomy is the deﬁnitive surgical treatment. Miotics are contraindicated and may worsen the episode.

question: Transscleral cyclophotocoagulation is most eﬀective in adult glaucoma patients when the laser is aimed approximately how far posterior to the limbus?
explanation: In transscleral cyclophotocoagulation, laser energy is applied to the secretory portion of the ciliary body (the pars plicata). The 810-nm diode laser is most commonly used for this procedure and the G probe, which is a ﬁberoptic handpiece that delivers the laser energy, centers 1.5 mm posterior to the limbus. In buphthalmic eyes where the limbus is stretched, the probe should be placed more posteriorly.

question: In the nonpenetrating glaucoma procedure depicted below, what is the purpose of the 10-0 polypropylene suture?

options.A: It is used to perform a goniotomy after canulation.
options.B: It is used to close the scleral ﬂaps.
options.C: It is used to locate the Schlemm canal and allow placement of viscoelastic.
options.D: It is tied with moderate tension to facilitate stretching of the Schlemm canal.

explanation: The correct answer is that 10-0 polypropylene suture will be left within the Schlemm canal and tied with moderate tension to stretch the Schlemm canal. Canaloplasty is a nonpenetrating glaucoma surgery, using a microcatheter through the Schlemm canal. The catheter is threaded for the full 360 degrees, then a 10-0 polypropylene suture is attached to the distal end of the catheter and the catheter is withdrawn while viscoelastic is injected, leaving the 10-0 polypropylene threaded within the Schlemm canal. The suture is tied with moderate BCSC Excerpt References Notes.

question: A patient presents with a peripherally and centrally shallow anterior chamber (AC) and increased intraocular pressure (IOP) after panretinal photocoagulation for proliferative diabetic retinopathy. In addition to aqueous suppression, what is an appropriate step in initial management?

options.C: intravitreal anti-vascular endothelial growth factor (anti-VEGF) injection

explanation: Angle closure after panretinal photocoagulation results from ciliary body swelling with anterior rotation of the lens-iris diaphragm. The AC is shallow both centrally and peripherally. Cycloplegia causes posterior movement of the iris-lens diaphragm, resulting in deepening of the AC. Laser iridotomy is not helpful, since there is no pupillary block. Laser iridoplasty may help to minimize iridocorneal contact but is not the ﬁrst step in management. Anti-VEGF injection is not helpful in addressing the mechanism of angle closure.

question: What procedure contracts collagen ﬁbers, pulling tissue away from the angle recess?
explanation: Peripheral iridoplasty is performed by using a thermal laser to treat the peripheral iris stroma. This causes contraction of collagen ﬁbers and thinning of the peripheral iris, pulling it away from the angle recess.

question: What artifact can be seen on visual ﬁeld testing if a patient's head moves back from the machine during the test?
explanation: It is important to assess for artifactual ﬁeld loss when assessing visual ﬁeld tests. If a lens is decentered, or a patient's head slides back from the forehead rest during the test, the lens rim can project into the central 30 degrees and cause a rim artifact. A cloverleaf pattern is BCSC Excerpt References Notes.

question: An 85-year-old pseudophakic woman requires surgery for advanced primary open-angle glaucoma (POAG) that is not controlled with maximum tolerated medical therapy. What factor in the patient's history could be a relative contraindication for trabeculectomy in this patient?

options.C: history of clear corneal cataract surgery

explanation: Surgical glaucoma treatment in the elderly requires consideration of several issues speciﬁc to this patient population. The need for surgery should ﬁrst be evaluated based on the severity of the disease, the risk of functional visual loss, the life expectancy of the patient, and the general condition and ability of the patient to withstand the stress of surgery. For trabeculectomy in particular, other considerations include the ability to adhere to the postoperative medical regimen, the ability to keep follow-up appointments, and the possibility of compromised healing, because the tissue of older patients is thinner and more fragile than that of younger patients. Frequent follow-up visits are critical in the postoperative management of trabeculectomy and therefore this procedure is best avoided if a patient is unable to come to the clinic for postoperative care. There is no speciﬁc age cut-oﬀ for the consideration of trabeculectomy. The success rate of trabeculectomy is lower in patients with cataract surgery via a scleral tunnel incision. Controlled hypertension is not a contraindication for glaucoma surgery.

question: What is the underlying mechanism of plateau iris syndrome?
explanation: Plateau iris conﬁguration is a narrow angle caused by anteriorly positioned ciliary processes that push the peripheral iris forward. In plateau iris syndrome, elevated intraocular pressure (IOP) and angle closure develop despite a patent iridotomy. Anterior iris insertions are often seen in anterior chamber developmental anomalies and congenital glaucoma. Anterior iris rotation may cause angle closure in aniridia.

question: What change in refractive error is typical in a patient taking pilocarpine?
explanation: Myopia caused by induced ciliary muscle contraction is a common side eﬀect of all cholinergic agents. This mechanism also causes headache/brow ache (from ciliary muscle spasm) in patients on pilocarpine therapy. Other long-term side eﬀects of pilocarpine include retinal detachment, cataract formation, iris pigment epithelial cysts, epiphora (lacrimal stimulation and punctal stenosis), and ocular surface changes (drug-induced pseudopemphigoid).

question: What form of secondary glaucoma is associated with higher rates of vitreous loss during cataract extraction?
explanation: Cataract extraction in the setting of pseudoexfoliation syndrome is more challenging and carries a higher rate of vitreous loss. Pupils often dilate poorly, making lens visualization more diﬃcult without pupil stretching. In addition, poor zonular support can make removal and placement of an IOL more diﬃcult. Postoperatively, there is a higher rate of capsular phimosis in these eyes. While pigment dispersion syndrome, steroid-induced glaucoma, and plateau iris syndrome do not predispose to vitreous loss, they are associated with selected other cataract surgery complications. For instance, one should be cognizant of protecting the cornea in the setting of a shallow chamber associated with plateau iris and reducing irrigation to prevent overdeepening of the anterior chamber in a myopic eye with pigment dispersion. 2 50 per pag.

question: By what mechanism do topical beta blockers reduce intraocular pressure?

options.A: reducing aqueous production by the ciliary body epithelium

explanation: Topical medications for the treatment of glaucoma can reduce the formation of aqueous and/or improve outﬂow of aqueous. Topical beta blockers reduce aqueous production by the ciliary epithelium by inhibiting cAMP production. This reduces aqueous secretion by 20% to 50%. Alpha agonists also reduce cAMP production via binding to the alpha 2 adrenoceptors. With long-term use, brimonidine has been shown to also increase uveoscleral outﬂow. Carbonic anhydrase inhibitors inhibit ciliary epithelium carbonic anhydrase, which reduces aqueous production. Parasympathomimetics cause contraction of the longitudinal ciliary muscle ﬁbers, which in turn increases outﬂow through the trabecular meshwork by causing tension on the scleral spur. Prostaglandin BCSC Excerpt References Notes.

question: What constitutes the classic clinical triad of primary congenital glaucoma?

options.A: photophobia, corneal edema, and corneal enlargement
options.B: corneal edema, Haab striae, and buphthalmos

explanation: Epiphora, photophobia, and blepharospasm constitute the classical clinical triad of primary congenital glaucoma. Other signs include clouding and enlargement of the cornea (ﬁrst ﬁgure). Photophobia, epiphora, and blepharospasm result from the glare and epithelial abnormalities associated with corneal edema and opaciﬁcation. Corneal edema results from elevated IOP and may be gradual or sudden in onset. Corneal edema is often the presenting sign in infants younger than 3 months. Microcystic edema initially involves the corneal epithelium but later extends to the stroma, often accompanied by one or more curvilinear breaks in Descemet membrane (Haab striae, second ﬁgure). Although the corneal edema may resolve with IOP reduction, a scar will remain permanently at the site of the Haab striae. A number of other conditions may also cause corneal edema or Descemet tears (such as birth trauma). Corneal enlargement occurs with gradual stretching of the cornea as a result of elevated IOP. A corneal diameter of greater than 11.5 mm is suggestive of glaucoma in a newborn, while a diameter greater than 12.5 mm suggests glaucoma at the age of 1 year. Glaucoma should be suspected in any child with a corneal diameter greater than 13.0 mm. Blepharophimosis is not a clinical feature of primary congenital glaucoma. ddd8- 4a80- aa92- cf6df0c063fb)  bb33- 55d6600bfb58) .

question: What corneal complication is most likely with the use of antiﬁbrotic agents for trabeculectomy?
explanation: Antiﬁbrotic agents, especially 5-ﬂuorouracil, are toxic to the corneal epithelium and can cause persistent corneal epithelial defects. Endothelial damage can occur with the use of antiﬁbrotics but is not common with the current surgical technique and dosage. Keratic precipitates and band keratopathy are not associated with the use of antiﬁbrotic agents.

question: An ophthalmologist examines an infant who has bilateral diﬀuse clouding, as shown. What is the most important initial measurement to obtain in managing this infant's condition?
explanation: The diﬀerential of this condition (bilateral cloudy corneas) is broad and includes congenital glaucoma, congenital hereditary endothelial dystrophy, congenital hereditary stromal dystrophy, and metabolic storage diseases. Although tests of corneal thickness, axial length, and refraction would be important to obtain, the one that would immediately change management is the measurement of IOP. Elevated IOP in an infant with cloudy corneas is consistent with congenital glaucoma and requires immediate action.

question: What is the cause of the hypertensive phase that may occur after tube shunt surgery?

options.B: decreased permeability of the capsule that forms around the end plate
options.C: overﬁltration through the lumen of the tube

explanation: Elevated intraocular pressure (IOP) in the early postoperative period can have various causes. The hypertensive phase is marked by a sudden elevation of IOP after previously well-functioning surgery. Usually occurring between 3 weeks and 3 months after surgery, it is caused by decreased permeability of the capsule that forms around the end plate. Over time, the hypertensive phase may resolve as the capsule reorganizes and becomes more permeable to aqueous. Choroidal eﬀusions may occur when IOP is low. Malignant glaucoma will have a shallow chamber with normal to high IOP. The chamber is very shallow centrally. Overﬁltration will cause low IOP.

question: A patient with a history of an occludable angle and glaucoma in his right eye is now 3 years status- post cataract surgery. On gonioscopy scleral spur is visible in 4/4 quadrants. His treated intraocular pressure (IOP) has been in the mid 20s on several visits, and he demonstrates visual ﬁeld, optical coherence tomography (OCT), and optic nerve changes consistent with progression of his disease over the past year. What is the most accurate classiﬁcation of this patient's glaucoma?
explanation: This patient's history of occludable angles and prior glaucoma suggests a component of angle-closure glaucoma in his history. Now, after cataract surgery, the patient has an anatomically open angle. However, his treated pressure continues to be elevated, with evidence of glaucomatous progression, suggesting persistently reduced outﬂow facility. As such, the most accurate classiﬁcation of his glaucoma is combined mechanism, because he seems to have progression of glaucomatous optic neuropathy despite anatomic correction of the occludable angle and he has persistently elevated IOP. Combined- mechanism glaucoma can also be used to refer to glaucoma in which several mechanisms are at play, for example primary open-angle glaucoma with superimposed neovascular glaucoma or primary open- angle glaucoma with a superimposed corticosteroid response or uveitic component. Primary open-angle glaucoma refers to glaucoma in which there is no physical obstruction of the trabecular meshwork visible at the gonioscopic level, and there is no underlying abnormality accounting for the condition. Secondary open-angle glaucoma refers to glaucoma in which a secondary condition (eg, corticosteroid-induced IOP elevation) accounts for impaired aqueous outﬂow in the setting of an anatomically open angle. Primary angle-closure glaucoma refers to glaucoma in which there is partial or complete obstruction of the angle by peripheral iris, either appositional or synechial, in the absence of an underlying condition.

question: Patients with the sporadic form of the iris abnormality shown in the image are at increased risk for what extraocular malignancy?
explanation: This image depicts aniridia. Although most cases of aniridia are inherited through autosomal dominant transmission, one-third of cases are isolated sporadic mutations, of which 20% are associated with an increased risk for Wilms tumor of the kidney. Wilms tumor results from a large chromosomal deletion, including the Wilms tumor 1 gene (WT1), a tumor suppressor gene. Colon cancer, brain tumors, and adrenal malignancies have not been linked to aniridia.

question: What systemic condition is associated with microspherophakia?
explanation: Weill-Marchesani syndrome is associated with short status, stocky body habitus, brachydactyly (short ﬁngers and toes), and microspherophakia. Homocystinuria, hyperlysinemia, and sulﬁte oxidase deﬁciency are all associated with intellectual disability. Patients with these conditions can develop ectopia lentis. Perform cataract surgery for phacomorphic glaucoma.

question: An 85-year-old woman had a laser peripheral iridotomy 2 days ago for acute angle closure, but her intraocular pressure is still elevated. She has mild cataracts in both eyes. What is your next step in management?

options.A: Perform cataract surgery for phacomorphic glaucoma.
options.B: Perform synechiolysis for chronic angle-closure glaucoma.
options.C: Administer topical steroids for phacolytic glaucoma.
options.D: Check for patency of iridotomy and repeat laser if it is not patent.

explanation: Of the nearly 67 million patients with glaucoma worldwide, it has been estimated that one-half are aﬀected by angle closure. Occurring less often in the West, it is the predominant form of glaucoma in East Asia. The presentation of angle closure can be acute, with profound symptoms, or chronic, with asymptomatic visual loss. The patient does not have a large lens, which could cause phacomorphic glaucoma, or a mature cataract, which could cause phacolytic glaucoma. She has acute, not chronic, angle closure. The most likely cause of persistent symptoms of angle closure following iridotomy in this patient is an iridotomy that is not patent. The procedure should be repeated if it is not patent.

question: What is the most common side eﬀect of oral carbonic anhydrase inhibitors (CAIs)?
explanation: Systemic side eﬀects are very common with oral CAIs. Almost all patients develop paresthesias of the ﬁngers and toes, usually without much functional impairment. Many patients develop fatigue and loss of appetite when using oral CAIs for more than a few days. Other common side eﬀects include gastric burning and irritation. CAIs decrease urinary concentration of citrate and magnesium and produce temporary urinary alkalinization, which favors formation of renal calculi. This side eﬀect usually occurs with prolonged treatment, and most calculi occur within the ﬁrst 12 months of treatment. Stevens-Johnson syndrome is a very rare but potentially fatal complication with oral CAIs, and patients should be warned to report skin rashes or mucous membrane changes, such as blisters or ulcers in the mouth.

question: What structure is indicated by the arrow (ﬁgure)?

options.A: thinning of the corneal stroma with lipid exudation
options.D: linear pattern of inﬂammatory cells on the endothelium

explanation: The photograph depicts a posterior embryotoxon, which appears as a thin, gray-white, arcuate line on the inner surface of the cornea. Anatomically, it signiﬁes an anteriorly displaced Schwalbe line, which is the junction between the Descemet membrane and the trabecular meshwork. A posterior embryotoxon may occur as an isolated ﬁnding, or it may be seen in conjunction with ocular anomalies like Axenfeld- Rieger and Alagille syndromes. When the posterior embryotoxon is BCSC Excerpt References Notes.

question: What tonometer type uses an annular ring to ﬂatten a small area of cornea, then measures the pressure at the center of the ﬂattened area, using a transducer?
explanation: A Mackay-Marg-type tonometer (eg, Tono-Pen, Reichert Technologies) uses an annular ring to ﬂatten a small area of cornea, then measures the pressure at the center of the ﬂattened area, using a transducer. These tonometers may be particularly useful in patients with corneal scars or edema, since the measurement tip is suﬃciently small to be applied only to normal parts of cornea, as necessary. An applanation tonometer (eg, Goldmann) measures the force necessary to ﬂatten a portion of the cornea, then applies the Imbert- Fick principle (Pressure = Force / Area) to determine intraocular pressure. An indentation tonometer (eg, Schiotz) determines intraocular pressure by measuring the amount of corneal indentation produced by a known weight. A rebound tonometer (eg, iCare) determines intraocular pressure by measuring the speed at which a small probe propelled against the cornea rebounds after impact.

question: What feature is common to all subtypes of iridocorneal endothelial (ICE) syndrome?
explanation: ICE syndrome is a group of disorders that includes essential iris atrophy, Chandler syndrome, and Cogan-Reese syndrome. All of these have abnormal endothelial cells with a "beaten bronze" appearance on slit-lamp examination. ICE syndrome is more common in women and commonly presents between 20 and 50 years of age. The condition is isolated to the eye, and is sporadic and unilateral.

question: A 2-year-old boy with congenital glaucoma presents for examination. Both corneas are cloudy, and his intraocular pressure (IOP) is 28 mm Hg in both eyes. What procedure would be the most suitable for this patient?
explanation: The correct answer is trabeculotomy. The presence of childhood glaucoma is an indication for surgery. Goniotomy and trabeculotomy are the preferred procedures. Goniotomy is possible only in an eye with a relative clear cornea, whereas trabeculotomy may be performed whether the cornea is clear or cloudy. For an eye that has failed these procedures, there is a debate whether the next step should be trabeculotomy or a glaucoma drainage device.

question: Open-angle glaucoma causes loss of what tissue layer(s) of the retina?

options.B: outer nuclear layer and photoreceptor layer
options.C: nerve ﬁber layer and ganglion cell layer
options.D: nerve ﬁber layer and inner nuclear layer

explanation: Open-angle glaucoma characteristically causes loss of the nerve ﬁber layer and ganglion cell layer, as illustrated in the ﬁgure. The remaining layers of the retina are normal. These pathologic changes explain the clinical ﬁndings of nerve ﬁber layer atrophy and eventual optic nerve changes. Experimental studies in primates show that the earliest structural changes in the retina with chronic elevation of intraocular pressure (IOP) are seen in the ganglion cell dendritic arbors and then the cell body. Eventually, the nerve axon (nerve ﬁber layer) degenerates. Today, optical coherence tomography (OCT) use to observe peripapillary retinal nerve ﬁber layer (RNFL) thickness has been established as a means of detecting and monitoring glaucoma. Recently, spectral-domain OCT (SD- OCT) has been used for quantitative assessment of macular thickness, with special attention to the macular RNFL, ganglion cell layer, and inner plexiform layer. However, whether this provides any advantages over assessment of the peripapillary RNFL is still under discussion. a158- 4e19- b652- 6a9a8214314d&t=636420407484570000)

question: Once the aqueous humor leaves the anterior chamber, what is the order of intraocular structures through which it passes in the pressure- sensitive outﬂow pathway?

options.A: corneoscleral trabecular meshwork, juxtacanalicular meshwork, uveal trabecular meshwork, outlet or collector channels, Schlemm canal, episcleral veins
options.B: ciliary muscle, Schlemm canal, outlet or collector channels, scleral wall
options.C: ciliary muscle, suprachoroidal space, scleral wall
options.D: uveal trabecular meshwork, corneoscleral trabecular meshwork, juxtacanalicular meshwork, Schlemm canal, outlet or collector channels, episcleral veins

explanation: There are 2 major paths the aqueous takes to exit the eye that include the pressure-sensitive trabecular outﬂow and the pressure-insensitive uveoscleral outﬂow. To recall which is which, remember that "sensitive" and "trabecular" start with consonants and "insensitive" and "uveoscleral" start with vowels. The pathway of aqueous through the pressure-sensitive trabecular outﬂow starts with the trabecular meshwork. The classically described layers of the trabecular meshwork are uveal (adjacent to anterior chamber, bands extending from the iris root/ciliary body to the peripheral cornea), corneoscleral (sheets of trabeculum from scleral spur to lateral wall of scleral sulcus), and juxtacanalicular (most outﬂow resistance, adjacent to/forms the inner wall of Schlemm canal). Of note, the trabecular cells are phagocytic, which is particularly relevant in the setting of inﬂammation and laser trabeculoplasty. (Mnemonic: Undercover job = uveal, corneoscleral, juxtacanalicular)

question: What is the critical slit-lamp ﬁnding in phacolytic glaucoma?

options.A: keratic precipitates on the corneal endothelium
options.B: large cells with debris and ﬂare in the anterior chamber

explanation: Phacolytic glaucoma is a complication of a mature or hypermature cataract in which denatured, high-molecular weight lens proteins leak through an intact but permeable lens capsule and induce inﬂammation and elevated intraocular pressure (IOP). The clinical presentation is typically an abrupt onset of pain and redness in an eye with prolonged poor vision. White debris and ﬂare are typical, but keratic precipitates, if found, are nonspeciﬁc. Phacolytic glaucoma is a form of secondary open-angle glaucoma. On gonioscopy, the angle is unaﬀected and usually of normal depth.

question: What is the most likely cause of this patient's gonioscopic ﬁndings?
explanation: Chronic angle-closure glaucoma (CACG), also known as creeping angle closure, is largely asymptomatic and is therefore often diagnosed in later stages, similar to primary open-angle glaucoma (POAG). It is a major cause of blindness in Asia. If gonioscopy is not performed, the diagnosis of CACG may be missed and the patient incorrectly labeled as having POAG. Treatment may involve laser peripheral iridotomy BCSC Excerpt References Notes.

question: What is the mode of inheritance for the genes that have been identiﬁed as associated with aniridia?
explanation: In general, the early-onset forms of glaucoma are rare and often follow patterns of simple Mendelian inheritance, with mutations that are highly penetrant. Aniridia is frequently associated with glaucoma. It occurs in an autosomal dominant (AD) inheritance pattern or sporadically. The AD form is associated with missense mutations in paired box gene 6 (PAX6), whereas the sporadic form is associated with large deletions or BCSC Excerpt References Notes.

question: What is the deﬁning abnormality seen in eyes with angle-recession glaucoma?

options.B: a tear in the ciliary body muscle

explanation: Traumatic recession of the anterior chamber angle is due to a tear in the ciliary body between the longitudinal and circular muscles, but only when there is concurrent damage to the meshwork does angle recession possibly lead to glaucoma. Iridodialysis is a rupture of the iris at the thinnest portion of the diaphragm, which does not cause glaucoma. Similarly, lens subluxation alone (without hemorrhage) does not cause glaucoma.

question: A patient whose intraocular pressure (IOP) is 36 mm Hg in one eye is referred by a retinal specialist to another ophthalmologist. The patient has history of exudative age- related macular degeneration and has been receiving intravitreal injections of bevacizumab for the past several years in that eye. No treatment to lower the IOP has been initiated yet. What is the best therapeutic option at this time for that purpose?
explanation: While the exact mechanism for IOP elevation remains unknown, there is a noted association in the literature between multiple anti-vascular endothelial growth factor (anti-VEGF) injections and chronic elevated IOP. Theories include inﬂammation and/or blockage of the trabecular meshwork. Based on this, the mechanism appears to be a secondary open-angle glaucoma; therefore, treatment with LPI would not be appropriate. Surgical therapy may be indicated in these patients if the IOP cannot be controlled medically and/or there are other contraindications to medical treatment. Generally, topical therapy is instituted before systemic therapy when attempting to lower IOP, because there is less potential for side eﬀects.

question: What is the most likely cause of elevated intraocular pressure in pseudoexfoliation glaucoma?

options.A: ﬁbrillar material obstructing the trabecular meshwork
options.B: ﬁbrillar material inducing peripheral anterior synechiae
options.C: ﬁbrillar material deposited on zonules with anterior rotation of the lens
options.D: ﬁbrillar material causing hypersecretion from the ciliary body

explanation: Pseudoexfoliation syndrome is thought to cause intraocular pressure elevation by obstruction of ﬂow through, and damage to the trabecular meshwork or the uveoscleral pathway from direct ﬁbrillar material deposition. Hypersecretion, pupillary block, and synechial closure of the angle are not the most common mechanisms of elevated intraocular pressure in pseudoexfoliation glaucoma. argon laser iridoplasty.

question: What is the treatment for a patient with elevated intraocular pressure and continued risk of angle closure despite patent peripheral iridotomy in plateau iris syndrome?
explanation: Plateau iris syndrome management initially includes either laser iridotomy to eliminate any component of pupillary block, or lensectomy can be considered if a cataract is present. Despite both of these treatments, plateau iris patients are at continued risk of angle closure secondary to the anterior insertion of the zonules on ciliary processes. Laser peripheral iridoplasty or argon gonioplasty is indicated in patients with a continued presence of a narrow angle despite patent iridotomy. Argon or selective laser trabeculoplasty would not decrease risk of angle closure. Repeat laser iridotomy would be indicated if the initial iridotomy had failed.

question: What side eﬀect is typically associated with prostaglandin analogues?
explanation: Prostaglandin analogues are very well tolerated as a class of hypotensive medications. Local side eﬀects are most common and include conjunctival hyperemia, hypertrichosis, and increased pigmentation of the iris and periocular skin. Less commonly, these drugs have been associated with cystoid macular edema, anterior uveitis, and reactivation of herpes simplex virus keratitis. While systemic side eﬀects are not frequent, ﬂu-like symptoms and joint/muscle pains can occur. Bitter taste is often associated with carbonic anhydrase inhibitors, decreased exercise tolerance is typically associated with beta-blockers, and dry mouth is associated with alpha- agonists.

question: A patient develops uncontrolled glaucoma several months after an extracapsular cataract extraction. A grayish, sheetlike opacity is noted on the superior corneal endothelial surface. What test will conﬁrm the diagnosis?
explanation: Argon laser can conﬁrm the diagnosis of epithelial ingrowth by producing white burns on the epithelial membrane and charcoal burns on normal iris surface. Extent of the ingrowth can also be demarcated by this method. Anterior chamber paracentesis (tap) is not indicated; it can deﬁne an infectious reaction rather than an inﬂammatory reaction with rise in intraocular pressure. Endothelial cell count may show a decreased cell number; however, specular microscopy would be a better diagnostic tool to deﬁne epithelial ingrowth, reversing the appearance of epithelial cells with dark centers and a lighter periphery. Gonioscopy to reveal retained lens fragments in the angle would not be likely to produce a ﬁnding of epithelial downgrowth, although it may reveal an epithelial sheet in the angle. The majority of cases of glaucoma caused by epithelial downgrowth have normal gonioscopic ﬁndings.

question: What type of tonometer uses the Imbert-Fick principle for measurement of intraocular pressure (IOP)?
explanation: Like the Goldmann tonometer, the Perkins tonometer is an applanation tonometer, and as such, is based on the Imbert-Fick principle. The Imbert-Fick principle relates the pressure inside a dry, thin-walled sphere to the force required to ﬂatten a speciﬁc area. The Goldmann applanation tonometer and the Perkins tonometer use the same measurement tip, which balances surface tension of the tear ﬁlm with the rigidity of the cornea to approximate a dry, inﬁnitely ﬂexible, thin- walled sphere for eyes with corneal thickness of 520 μm. decreased aqueous humor production B. 2% resultant renal metabolic acidosis, which reduces activity of ciliary epithelial function C. 1% vitreous dehydration and shrinkage D. 93%.

question: What is the mechanism by which topical carbonic anhydrase inhibitor therapy decreases intraocular pressure?

options.B: increased aqueous humor outﬂow through the trabecular meshwork
options.C: increased aqueous humor outﬂow via the uveoscleral pathway
options.D: creation of an osmotic gradient to reduce intraocular ﬂuid volume

explanation: Topical carbonic anhydrase inhibitors (eg, dorzolamide) decrease aqueous humor production by the ciliary epithelium, thus decreasing intraocular pressure. Parasympathomimetic agents (eg, pilocarpine) and Rho kinase inhibitors (eg, netarsudil) increase trabecular outﬂow. Prostaglandin analogues (eg, latanoprost) increase uveoscleral outﬂow. Hyperosmotic agents (eg, mannitol) increase blood osmolality, thus creating an osmotic gradient to draw water from the eye. tube shunt surgery.

question: In a frail elderly patient who is not mobile, what procedure for open- angle glaucoma would be a good choice because it requires a smaller number of postoperative visits than some other surgeries?
explanation: When deciding whether to perform surgery in a frail elderly patient, the surgeon must consider issues speciﬁc to this population. Once the decision has been made to proceed with surgery, the surgeon should determine which procedure is most likely to be adequately successful in reducing IOP with the fewest possible complications. If a patient is not mobile or lacks easy transportation options, a nonpenetrating surgery, minimally invasive glaucoma surgery (MIGS), or a cyclodestructive procedure may be preferred, as these procedures require fewer postoperative visits than does a trabeculectomy or a tube shunt surgery. Iridoplasty is not used to treat open-angle glaucoma.

question: A 47-year-old woman is diagnosed with normal-tension glaucoma and treatment is initiated. What should the target intraocular pressure (IOP) percent reduction be for this patient?
explanation: Normal-tension (low-tension) glaucoma is thought to be multifactorial in its etiology, and the mechanism for disease progression is not fully understood. However, results from the Collaborative Normal-Tension Glaucoma Study (CNTGS) demonstrate that aggressive IOP lowering can lessen the risk of progression in these patients over a 5-year period. The study aimed for at least 30% IOP reduction from baseline, and in those patients, the risk of visual ﬁeld progression was decreased from 35% to 12%. A caveat of this ﬁnding is that about half of patients who did not receive treatment over the 5-year period did not progress, making it likely that IOP is not the only factor in the development and progression of normal-tension glaucoma.

question: What is the typical angle appearance on gonioscopy in primary congenital glaucoma?

options.A: deep chamber with high iris insertion
options.B: deep chamber with heavy trabecular meshwork (TM) pigmentation
options.C: deep chamber with iris adhesions to the Schwalbe line

explanation: Infants with primary congenital glaucoma typically have deep anterior chambers with a high, ﬂat anterior iris insertion. The peripheral iris may be hypoplastic. Iris adhesions and a prominent embryotoxon may be seen with Axenfeld-Rieger syndrome. A heavily pigmented TM may be seen in pigmentary glaucoma but is not a feature of any infantile glaucoma. refractive error.

question: What factor can lead to the type of visual ﬁeld shown in the ﬁgure?

options.C: centering the patient away from the correcting lens

explanation: This visual ﬁeld is a rim artifact defect secondary to improper positioning of the patient relative to a correcting lens. Many factors may aﬀect the results obtained from perimetry, including the patient's level of alertness, the perimetrist's administration of the test, interaction between patient and perimetrist, refractive error, pupil size ( <2.5mm), use of miotics such as pilocarpine, and care in centering the patient close to the correcting lens to avoid lens rim artifact where the rim blocks the peripheral stimuli.

question: A 7-year-old child is referred for evaluation with history of a port- wine stain involving the right eyelids and side of face. A complete ocular examination is performed, and elevated intraocular pressure is noted in the right eye. What additional testing is the most important next step in the management of this patient?
explanation: There is concern for Sturge-Weber syndrome, also known as encephalotrigeminal angiomatosis, in this patient. There is no race or gender predilection and no inheritance pattern has been established for this condition. Genetic testing is unlikely to be helpful. Patients can also have an ipsilateral choroidal hemangioma, causing a "tomato ketchup" fundus appearance, and characterization with ICG may be useful. Most importantly, there is an association with ipsilateral leptomeningeal angioma, which can lead to intracerebral calciﬁcations, seizures, focal neurologic deﬁcits, and a variable amount of cognitive impairment. A systemic workup with neurorimaging is therefore of key importance.

question: What class of glaucoma medication has been associated with an increased risk of post- cataract surgery cystoid macular edema (CME)?
explanation: Prostaglandin analogue use has been associated with CME, especially in high-risk eyes (ie, aphakic eyes, pseudophakic eyes with open posterior capsules, and eyes with uveitis). The use of beta blockers, alpha agonists, and carbonic anhydrase inhibitors is not associated with CME.

question: A patient with a history of piggyback intraocular lenses (IOL) in the left eye, both placed within the capsular bag, is referred by a local optometrist for evaluation of elevated intraocular pressure in that eye. Endothelial pigment deposition is noted on slit-lamp examination. What gonioscopic ﬁnding might be expected in this scenario?
explanation: Interlenticular opaciﬁcation and iris chaﬁng are possible complications seen with implantation of piggyback intraocular lenses within the capsular bag. Iris chaﬁng can result in a pigment dispersion syndrome, and associated elevated intraocular pressure, presumably from obstruction of the trabecular meshwork by pigment granules. Findings associated with pigment dispersion syndrome include pigment deposits on the corneal endothelium (Krukenberg spindle), midperipheral iris transillumination defects, pigment staining of the lens capsule at the insertion of the zonular ﬁbers (Zentmayer ring or Scheie stripe), heavy pigmentation of the trabecular meshwork, and pigment speckling at or anterior to the Schwalbe line (Sampaolesi line).

question: What is the desired observed treatment eﬀect during endocyclophotocoagulation (ECP)?
explanation: Endoscopic cyclophotocoagulation is performed through a clear corneal or limbal incision with direct visualization of the ciliary processes. Power is titrated to achieve shrinking and whitening of the ciliary processes. Bubble formation and ciliary process rupture should be avoided to minimize postoperative inﬂammation. Photocoagulation lightens rather than darkens the tissue.

question: According to the Goldmann equation, what is the ratio of increase in intraocular pressure (IOP) to the increase in episcleral venous pressure in millimeters of mercury (mm Hg)?
explanation: According to the Goldmann equation, where P = (F - U)/C + P where P is the IOP in mm Hg, F is the rate of aqueous formation, U is the rate of aqueous humor drainage through the pressure-insensitive uveoscleral pathway in microliters per minute (μL/min), C is the facility of outﬂow through the pressure-sensitive trabecular pathway in microliters per minute per mm Hg (μL/min/mm Hg ) and P is the episcleral venous pressure in mm Hg, the IOP rises 1 mm Hg for every 1 mm Hg of rise in episcleral venous pressure. Patients with Sturge-Weber, carotid-cavernous sinus ﬁstulas, cavernous sinus thrombosis, and thyroid eye disease (partial increase) have increased episcleral venous pressure from obstruction of venous return o v o v BCSC Excerpt References Notes.

question: A patient presents with approximately 360 degrees of synechial closure on gonioscopy. There is no history of trauma, uveitis, or other predisposing conditions for synechial formation. The intraocular pressure (IOP) is 21 mm Hg (normal corneal pachymetry). There is mild nerve ﬁber layer (NFL) thinning on optical coherence tomography (OCT) and no deﬁcits noted on standard perimetry. What is the best next course of action to manage this patient?
explanation: This patient appears to have chronic angle-closure glaucoma. There is no clear secondary etiology for the synechial formation, and the patient does not have an acutely elevated IOP. Because of the extensive peripheral anterior synechiae (PAS) on gonioscopy, LPI (laser peripheral iridotomy) may not be successful in increasing outﬂow in the angle, and treatment could result in excessive pigment release, inﬂammation, and IOP spike. Medical therapy may work in these patients, but depending on the level of impaired trabecular outﬂow, surgical intervention in the form of ﬁltering surgery may be required at some point. Given the early signs of optic nerve damage on imaging, observation is not the best next step.

question: What parasympathomimetic medication has both direct and indirect parasympathomimetic activity?
explanation: Direct-acting parasympathomimetic agents directly stimulate motor end plates (pilocarpine, acetylcholine chloride). Indirect-acting agents inhibit acetylcholinesterase, increasing the availability of acetylcholine at motor end plates (echothiophate iodide). Carbachol has both direct and indirect parasympathomimetic activity.

question: In the treatment of primary congenital glaucoma, what is an advantage of a goniotomy over trabeculotomy?

options.A: It can be easily converted to a trabeculectomy if the Schlemm canal cannot be cannulated
options.B: There is no postoperative conjunctival scarring.
options.C: Intraocular pressure (IOP) lowering typically lasts longer.
options.D: A surgical approach is not hindered by opaciﬁed corneas.

explanation: In primary congenital glaucoma (PCG), medical management is the usual treatment until surgical intervention can occur. An ab interno goniotomy or an ab externo trabeculotomy are usually the ﬁrst surgeries of choice. The success rates and IOP-lowering eﬀects are similar for these surgeries. Because a goniotomy is performed through a corneal incision and through the anterior chamber, no postoperative conjunctival scarring occurs, which is preferable if further incisional glaucoma surgery is needed in the future. However, goniotomy requires a clear cornea to obtain an adequate view. A trabeculotomy can be easily converted into a trabeculectomy, given their similar dissection.

question: An infant is scheduled for an examination under anesthesia. What anesthetic agent would have the least eﬀect on the infant's intraocular pressure (IOP)?
explanation: Most anesthetics have an eﬀect on IOP measurements. Sevoﬂurane and many others lower IOP, whereas ketamine and succinylcholine (not really an anesthetic agent, but a skeletal muscle relaxant adjunct to general anesthesia) may increase IOP. Chloral hydrate has been shown to have no eﬀect on IOP measurement.

question: What is the likely cause of increased intraocular pressure in the setting of chronic vitreous hemorrhage?

options.B: "ghost cell" degeneration of red blood cells

explanation: Red blood cells (RBCs) in the vitreous cavity may undergo degenerative changes. Clots undergo ﬁbrinolysis and RBCs may diﬀuse throughout the vitreous after 3 to 10 days, with the development of RBC degeneration. Hemoglobin leaks from the RBC change the normally biconcave pliable cells to spherical, hollow, khaki-colored, BCSC Excerpt References Notes.

question: A 60-year-old woman with history of primary angle-closure glaucoma, status post successful laser peripheral iridotomy in the past, has uncontrolled intraocular pressure (IOP) on medical treatment. The visual acuity is 20/25, there is synechial angle closure for 270 degrees, and the cup-to-disc (C:D) ratio is 0.9. What is the most appropriate intervention for this patient?
explanation: Glaucoma ﬁltration surgery is indicated for IOP lowering in this patient with extensive synechial angle closure and advanced cupping of the optic nerve. Iridotomy will not alter angle anatomy or lower IOP in the presence of extensive synechial closure and is not indicated. Trabeculoplasty is potentially feasible in only 90 degrees of the angle and would not likely provide adequate IOP lowering with such a small area of treatment. Cyclophotocoagulation can be employed for IOP control in refractory glaucoma but is not indicated as the ﬁrst surgical intervention in this patient. A high temporal frequency counter phase ﬂicker stimulus is used.

question: What is the stimulus used to test the peripheral visual ﬁeld in frequency-doubling technology (FDT) perimetry ?

options.A: A high temporal frequency counter phase ﬂicker stimulus is used.
options.B: A kinetic stimulus is moved from a non-seeing to a seeing area of the visual ﬁeld.
options.C: A stationary stimulus of varying intensity is presented at predetermined locations to measure threshold.
options.D: A blue stimulus is projected onto a yellow background.

explanation: FDT perimetry is a visual ﬁeld testing paradigm that uses low spatial sinusoidal grating undergoing rapid-phase reversal ﬂicker. SITA SWAP (Swedish interactive thresholding algorithm short-wavelength automated perimetry) testing employs a blue light stimulus on a yellow background for early glaucoma detection. Kinetic perimetry involves moving a target from a non-seeing to a seeing area. Static perimetry varies a stationary stimulus at locations and changes the brightness, size, and duration of the stimulus to determine the threshold.

question: What cause of leukocoria is associated with microphthalmos?
explanation: Each of the answer choices (Coats disease, retinoblastoma, persistent fetal vasculature, and Toxocara species) can cause unilateral leukocoria. However, only persistent fetal vasculature is associated with microphthalmos.
